title: The Company That Sells You Nothing

beats.name: COLD OPEN / THE EMPTY GYM
beats.vo: Planet Fitness has about twenty point eight million members. It has roughly two thousand eight hundred and ninety-six clubs.
beats.visual: B-roll: COLD OPEN / THE EMPTY GYM
beats.question: How can a gym support this many members?
beats.reveal: The empty room is the contradiction: huge membership, limited physical capacity.
beats.footage: empty gym interior, dim lighting, rows of treadmills, lone person

beats.name: THE IMPOSSIBLE RATIO
beats.vo: That's around seven thousand two hundred members per location. A typical gym is twenty thousand square feet, and the fire code puts the maximum occupancy somewhere between two hundred and three hundred and fifty people.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — THE IMPOSSIBLE RATIO
beats.question: What if low attendance is not a failure?
beats.reveal: Capacity math: 7,200 members per club against 200–350 per room.

beats.name: THE FIRE CODE
beats.vo: So if four percent of the members of a single Planet Fitness showed up on the same evening, the fire marshal would close it. If ten percent showed up, the business would not survive the month.
beats.visual: Two-sided contradiction card — THE FIRE CODE
beats.question: What would happen if members actually came?
beats.reveal: 4% of members would trip the fire marshal; 10% would kill the business.

beats.name: THIS IS THE PRODUCT
beats.vo: This is not a risk the company manages. It's the product.
beats.visual: Closing payoff card — THIS IS THE PRODUCT
beats.question: What is the business actually selling?
beats.reveal: Not managing the risk — selling the absence of customers.

beats.name: THE $86 ESTIMATE
beats.vo: Here's a number that should bother you more than it does. When researchers asked Americans how much they spend every month on subscriptions, the average guess was eighty-six dollars.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — THE $86 ESTIMATE
beats.question: What do people think subscriptions cost?
beats.reveal: The average guess: $86 a month — C+R Research survey.

beats.name: THE $219 REALITY
beats.vo: Then they walked the same people through it category by category. Streaming. Music. Cloud storage. The gym. The app you downloaded for a trip in 2023. The real figure was two hundred and nineteen.
beats.visual: Two-sided contradiction card — THE $219 REALITY
beats.question: What do the same people actually spend?
beats.reveal: Itemizing the same people: $219 — $133 more than they guessed.

beats.name: THE $133 GAP
beats.vo: A hundred and thirty-three dollars a month, sixteen hundred dollars a year, going somewhere they couldn't name. More than half of people underestimate by at least a hundred dollars. Around four in ten are still paying for something they've forgotten they have.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — THE $133 GAP
beats.question: Where does the forgotten money go?
beats.reveal: 54% underestimate by $100+; 4 in 10 still pay for something forgotten.

beats.name: SOMEBODY BUILT IT
beats.vo: That gap is not carelessness. Somebody built it. It took about thirty years, it happened in public, and by the time anyone tried to stop it, it was the default way almost everything in America gets sold. This is how that happened.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — SOMEBODY BUILT IT
beats.question: Is the gap an accident?
beats.reveal: The gap was built in public over thirty years — then it became the default.
beats.footage: vintage advertisements, 1990s magazine ads, subscription fine print

beats.name: START WITH THE GYM
beats.vo: Start with the gym, because the gym is where the model is easiest to see.
beats.visual: B-roll: START WITH THE GYM
beats.question: Where does the model become visible?
beats.reveal: The gym makes the economics visible without hiding behind software.
beats.footage: gym interior, exercise machines, bright lights

beats.name: FIXED COSTS
beats.vo: A gym has a strange cost structure. The building costs the same whether one person walks in or a thousand do. The machines cost the same. The lease, the lights, the insurance, the staff at the desk — all of it is fixed.
beats.visual: Rising line chart, paper background — FIXED COSTS
beats.question: Why is a gym's cost structure strange?
beats.reveal: Building, machines, lease, lights, staff — fixed whether one or a thousand walk in.

beats.name: PURE PROFIT UNTIL THEY TURN UP
beats.vo: Which means every additional member is almost pure profit — right up until the moment they actually turn up. Then they need a machine, and a shower, and space on the floor, and the economics invert.
beats.visual: Trend chart, paper background — PURE PROFIT UNTIL THEY TURN UP
beats.question: When does a member stop being pure profit?
beats.reveal: The economics invert the moment the member actually consumes.

beats.name: THE IDEAL CUSTOMER
beats.vo: So the ideal customer is obvious. It's the one who pays and doesn't come.
beats.visual: B-roll: THE IDEAL CUSTOMER
beats.question: Who is the ideal customer?
beats.reveal: The one who pays and never walks in.
beats.footage: person walking past gym entrance, not going in

beats.name: TWO-THIRDS UNUSED
beats.vo: Industry estimates put the share of gym memberships that go essentially unused at up to two-thirds. Some of those people intend to go. Most of them intended to go in January.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — TWO-THIRDS UNUSED
beats.question: How common is non-use?
beats.reveal: Up to two-thirds of memberships go essentially unused; most intended to go in January.

beats.name: BREAKAGE
beats.vo: There's a word for revenue a company collects for a service it never has to deliver. Breakage.
beats.visual: Closing payoff card — BREAKAGE
beats.question: What is revenue for a service never delivered called?
beats.reveal: Breakage — the word from the gift-card business.

beats.name: GIFT CARDS / MILES / CREDIT
beats.vo: It came from the gift card business. A card gets bought, partly spent, thrown in a drawer, and the unspent balance eventually becomes profit that cost nothing to produce. Airlines have it with expired miles. Retailers have it with store credit.
beats.visual: Icon card — GIFT CARDS / MILES / CREDIT
beats.question: Where did breakage come from?
beats.reveal: Gift cards, expired miles, store credit — but each breaks only once.

beats.name: EVERY MONTH, FOREVER
beats.vo: But a gift card only breaks once. A subscription breaks every single month, forever, until somebody actively stops it.
beats.visual: Chronological timeline — EVERY MONTH, FOREVER
beats.question: How is subscription breakage different?
beats.reveal: A subscription breaks every month until someone actively stops it.

beats.name: BALLY / THE OLD MODEL
beats.vo: The first companies to industrialise this got it wrong, and the way they got it wrong is instructive. Through the nineties, the dominant American gym chain was Bally. And Bally's approach to keeping revenue was not subtle. It used long contracts — customers who believed they were signing up for a few months of access found they had committed to three years — and it enforced them.
beats.visual: B-roll: BALLY / THE OLD MODEL
beats.question: Who industrialised this first?
beats.reveal: Bally: long contracts, three-year commitments, enforced.
beats.footage: 1990s gym interior, retro exercise equipment, neon lighting

beats.name: THE 1994 INVESTIGATION
beats.vo: In 1994, federal regulators investigated the company's billing practices, including charges customers said they never authorised and contract terms that made cancellation far harder than it appeared. It settled, paid a civil penalty, and issued refunds without admitting wrongdoing.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — THE 1994 INVESTIGATION
beats.question: What happened when regulators looked at Bally?
beats.reveal: 1994: federal investigation, settled with a penalty and refunds, no admission.
beats.footage: federal documents, investigation file, courtroom

beats.name: 600+ COMPLAINTS
beats.vo: That did not end it. A decade later, the New York Attorney General opened an investigation after more than six hundred consumer complaints — people describing advertisements that promised short-term access and delivered three-year obligations, and cancellations that were submitted and then simply not honoured. Bally settled that too, agreeing to a set of reforms: a grace period, clearer cancellation procedures, pro-rata refunds.
beats.visual: B-roll: 600+ COMPLAINTS
beats.question: Did the first settlement end it?
beats.reveal: A decade later: NY AG, 600+ complaints, reforms — grace period, clearer cancellation, pro-rata refunds.
beats.footage: stack of complaint letters, government office building

beats.name: THE VICTIM WITH A DOCUMENT
beats.vo: Now, read what happened next as a business lesson rather than a morality tale, because that's how the industry read it. Bally's model worked, in the narrow sense that it extracted money from people who had stopped attending. But it worked by creating a legal obligation — and a legal obligation generates something dangerous. It generates a victim who can point at a document and say: I tried to leave, and you wouldn't let me.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — THE VICTIM WITH A DOCUMENT
beats.question: Why was the contract dangerous?
beats.reveal: A legal obligation creates a victim who can point at a document.
beats.footage: contract document close-up, signature line, fine print

beats.name: THE CONTRACT WAS THE WRONG TOOL
beats.vo: That produces complaints. Complaints produce attorneys general. Attorneys general produce settlements. So the next generation of the model removed the contract.
beats.visual: Closing payoff card — THE CONTRACT WAS THE WRONG TOOL
beats.text: THE CONTRACT WAS THE WRONG TOOL
beats.question: What did the industry learn?
beats.reveal: Complaints → attorneys general → settlements — so the next generation removed the contract.

beats.name: PLANET FITNESS REVERSAL
beats.vo: Planet Fitness will let you cancel. There's no three-year term to escape and no collections agency waiting. On paper it is the most consumer-friendly gym in America — which is exactly the point, because it discovered something the lawyers at Bally never understood.
beats.visual: B-roll: PLANET FITNESS REVERSAL
beats.question: What replaced the contract?
beats.reveal: Planet Fitness: no contract, no collections — friction instead of legal obligation.
beats.footage: modern gym entrance, front desk, membership card

beats.name: LEAVING IS NOT WORTH YOUR AFTERNOON
beats.vo: You don't need to trap somebody if leaving is simply not worth their afternoon.
beats.visual: B-roll: LEAVING IS NOT WORTH YOUR AFTERNOON
beats.question: Why not trap people?
beats.reveal: You don't need a trap if leaving isn't worth the afternoon.
beats.footage: person at gym front desk, cancelling membership, paperwork

beats.name: $10 BELOW THE THRESHOLD
beats.vo: And here's the part that took real intelligence to figure out. If you want to maximise breakage, the worst thing you can do is charge a lot. Charge ninety-nine dollars a month and people notice. It shows up on the statement, it sits there looking expensive, and one Sunday afternoon somebody decides to deal with it. Charge ten dollars a month, and something different happens. Ten dollars is below the threshold where the effort of cancelling feels worth it. To end it you'd need to find the login you set up on a different phone, remember which email you used, sit through the retention screens. Twenty minutes of irritation to recover ten dollars.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — $10 BELOW THE THRESHOLD
beats.question: What is the worst price to charge?
beats.reveal: $99 gets noticed; $10 sits below the effort threshold of cancelling.

beats.name: THE $120 / YEAR PUNCH
beats.vo: Most people, correctly, decide that's a bad trade. So they keep paying — not because they can't afford to stop, but because stopping costs more than continuing.
beats.visual: Two-sided contradiction card — THE $120 / YEAR PUNCH
beats.question: How do small charges compound?
beats.reveal: People keep paying because stopping costs more than continuing.

beats.name: THE INTENTION PRODUCT
beats.vo: The gym isn't selling you fitness. It's selling you the intention to get fit, and then quietly billing you for the gap between that intention and your actual Tuesday evening.
beats.visual: Icon card — THE INTENTION PRODUCT
beats.question: What is the gym actually selling?
beats.reveal: Not fitness — the intention to get fit, billed against your Tuesday evening.

beats.name: THEY JUST MADE IT VISIBLE
beats.vo: The gyms didn't invent this. They just made it visible. Because at almost exactly the moment the fitness industry perfected the model, an entirely different kind of company was looking at the same maths — and it was about to apply it to something you already owned.
beats.visual: B-roll: THEY JUST MADE IT VISIBLE
beats.question: Did the gyms invent this?
beats.reveal: The gyms made the model visible — software was about to apply it to what you owned.
beats.footage: modern gym, rows of machines, empty treadmill

beats.name: BUYING SOFTWARE LIKE AN APPLIANCE
beats.vo: For about twenty years, buying software worked like buying anything else. You paid Adobe roughly seven hundred dollars for Photoshop. A box arrived. Inside was a disc and a licence key, and that key was yours. Not rented — yours. You could use that copy in 2005 and you could still use it in 2015. If Adobe went out of business, the disc still worked.
beats.visual: B-roll: BUYING SOFTWARE LIKE AN APPLIANCE
beats.question: How did software ownership work?
beats.reveal: Buy once — disc, licence key — yours, even if Adobe went out of business.
beats.footage: software box, CD-ROM, old computer monitor, retail shelf

beats.name: THE SAWTOOTH REVENUE
beats.vo: The problem, from Adobe's side, was that chart. Revenue arrived in spikes. Every eighteen to twenty-four months they'd ship a new version, everybody would upgrade, and then there'd be a long flat stretch where a designer with a working copy of CS4 had no particular reason to give Adobe another dollar.
beats.visual: Trend chart, paper background — THE SAWTOOTH REVENUE
beats.question: What was Adobe's problem?
beats.reveal: Upgrade spikes then flat stretches — the customer had no reason to re-buy.

beats.name: MAY 6, 2013
beats.vo: Worse, the software had become good enough. By 2012, Photoshop could already do essentially everything a working professional needed. Adobe was in the uncomfortable position of having to invent reasons for people to re-buy a tool that wasn't broken. On the sixth of May, 2013, Adobe announced that Creative Suite was finished. Not discounted. Not deprioritised. Finished. There would be no CS7. From that point forward, the only way to get Photoshop was Creative Cloud — a monthly subscription that never ended and never became yours.
beats.visual: Chronological timeline — MAY 6, 2013
beats.question: What did Adobe announce?
beats.reveal: Creative Suite finished. No CS7. Only Creative Cloud — a subscription that never ends.

beats.name: THE BACKLASH
beats.vo: The reaction was genuinely furious. A petition demanding Adobe reverse the decision gathered tens of thousands of signatures. The tech press called it hostage-taking. Professional designers pointed out the obvious thing: under the old model, if you stopped paying, you kept your tools. Under the new one, if you stopped paying, twenty years of your work became files you could no longer open. Adobe did it anyway.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — THE BACKLASH
beats.question: How did customers react?
beats.reveal: Furious: petition, hostage-taking press, files you could no longer open. Adobe did it anyway.
beats.footage: angry internet forum, news headlines, petition

beats.name: THE NUMBERS
beats.vo: Here's what happened. Adobe's subscription revenue in 2013 was about one point two three billion dollars. By 2023 it was eighteen point two eight billion. Total company revenue went from roughly four point four billion before the transition to over fifteen billion. Creative Cloud went from zero subscribers to more than thirty million.
beats.visual: Trend chart, paper background — THE NUMBERS
beats.question: Did the model work financially?
beats.reveal: Subscription revenue $1.23B (2013) → $18.28B (2023); company revenue $4.4B → $15B+; 30M+ subscribers.

beats.name: NOT 15× BETTER
beats.vo: And notice what did not cause that. Adobe did not fifteen-times its revenue by making Photoshop fifteen times better. The software improved, but not like that. Nobody looks at Photoshop in 2023 and sees fifteen versions of the 2013 program. What changed was the ownership. Adobe took a thing you bought once and converted it into a thing you rent forever — and in doing so, converted a customer who might return into a customer who has to keep paying to keep what they've already made.
beats.visual: Two-sided contradiction card — NOT 15× BETTER
beats.question: What actually changed?
beats.reveal: Not the product — the ownership. Bought once became rented forever.

beats.name: THE BACKLASH DOESN'T MATTER
beats.vo: That result did not go unnoticed. Because the lesson every other company in America took from Adobe was not make better products. It was simpler than that, and much worse: the backlash doesn't matter. People were angry, they signed the petition, they wrote the posts — and then they subscribed.
beats.visual: B-roll: THE BACKLASH DOESN'T MATTER
beats.question: What did other companies learn?
beats.reveal: The lesson taken: the backlash doesn't matter — people subscribed anyway.
beats.footage: person typing on laptop, subscription website

beats.name: STREAMING RESET
beats.vo: The clearest proof that the model won isn't in software at all. It's in the thing that was supposed to be the model's opposite.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — STREAMING RESET
beats.question: Where is the model's clearest proof?
beats.reveal: The thing that was supposed to be the opposite of subscriptions.
beats.footage: television remote on sofa, streaming apps on screen

beats.name: THE BUNDLE
beats.vo: For years, the argument against cable television was the bundle. You paid one large monthly bill for two hundred channels, watched about nine of them, and had no way to pay for only the nine. It was the most resented recurring charge in the American household, and streaming was sold explicitly as the escape from it. Pay for what you want. Cancel any time. No contract, no box, no installer.
beats.visual: B-roll: THE BUNDLE
beats.question: What was the argument against cable?
beats.reveal: 200 channels, watched 9 — the most resented recurring charge; streaming sold as the escape.
beats.footage: cable box, television, remote control, tangled cables

beats.name: THE CATALOGUE SPLITS
beats.vo: And for a while it was exactly that. Then every studio worked out that licensing its catalogue to Netflix was worth less than launching its own service — so the catalogue split. The show you wanted moved. Then another one moved. And the only way to watch what you used to watch was to hold four or five subscriptions at once.
beats.visual: Icon card — THE CATALOGUE SPLITS
beats.question: What happened to the escape?
beats.reveal: Studios kept their catalogues; the show moved; now four or five subscriptions at once.

beats.name: THE NEW BUNDLE
beats.vo: By 2025, survey work put the average American household at roughly four point seven streaming services, paying about sixty-one dollars a month combined — up from around forty-eight two years earlier, as essentially every major platform raised prices. Add a live-TV service on top, which many households do to get sports, and the total moves past a hundred and twenty dollars.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — THE NEW BUNDLE
beats.question: Did streaming rebuild the bundle?
beats.reveal: By 2025: 4.7 services / $61 a month — JD Power 2025, up from $48 two years earlier.

beats.name: SIX SMALL BILLS
beats.vo: Which is roughly what cable cost. The industry rebuilt the bundle. Same total, same monthly recurrence, same resentment — except now it arrives as five or six separate charges instead of one, which is the important difference. One large bill is a thing you argue with. Six small ones are a thing you stop noticing.
beats.visual: Two-sided contradiction card — SIX SMALL BILLS
beats.question: What did the industry rebuild?
beats.reveal: One large bill is a thing you argue with. Six small ones are a thing you stop noticing.

beats.name: STREAMFLATION
beats.vo: There's a term for the mechanism, coined as it was happening: streamflation. Every service raises its price modestly, independently, at a moment when cancelling that one service still feels petty. None of the increases is worth acting on alone. Together, they reassembled the exact bill everybody had left.
beats.visual: Rising line chart, paper background — STREAMFLATION
beats.question: What mechanism reassembled the bill?
beats.reveal: Each modest price rise alone feels petty; together they rebuild the exact bill you left.

beats.name: THE MODEL EVERYWHERE
beats.vo: Within a few years the model was everywhere. Software, obviously. But then cars, where BMW briefly tried charging a monthly fee to switch on heated seats that were already installed in the vehicle you'd bought. Printers, where the machine watches how much you print and bills you for it. Kitchen appliances. Doorbells. Features in things you own, waiting behind a monthly payment. And once everything is a subscription, one thing becomes far more valuable than any product decision a company can make. Making it hard to leave.
beats.visual: Icon card — THE MODEL EVERYWHERE
beats.question: Where did the model spread?
beats.reveal: Cars, printers, doorbells, appliances — features in things you own. Making it hard to leave is the product.

beats.name: FTC SUES AMAZON
beats.vo: In 2023, the Federal Trade Commission sued Amazon. The allegation was not about prices, or competition, or warehouses. It was about a button. The FTC's case was that Amazon had designed its checkout so that customers enrolled in Prime without understanding they'd done it — using what regulators call dark patterns. Not lies. Design. A layout where the expensive choice is the easy one and the free choice is a small grey line of text you have to look for.
beats.visual: B-roll: FTC SUES AMAZON
beats.question: What was the FTC's case about?
beats.reveal: Enrollment without understanding — dark patterns: the expensive choice is the easy one.
beats.footage: federal building columns, courthouse, online shopping checkout

beats.name: MILLIONS PAYING
beats.vo: Millions of people, the FTC alleged, were paying for a subscription they never knowingly agreed to start. But that wasn't the part that made the case famous. The famous part was what happened when those customers tried to cancel.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — MILLIONS PAYING
beats.question: How many people were affected?
beats.reveal: Millions paying for a subscription they never knowingly started — but the famous part was cancelling.
beats.footage: credit card statement, bank account app, subscription charges

beats.name: THE CANCELLATION MAZE
beats.vo: To leave Prime, a customer had to move through a sequence of pages. Each one confirmed they wanted to cancel. Each one offered a reason to stay. Discounts, pauses, reminders of benefits they'd lose. At several points the button that continued the cancellation was smaller and paler than the button that abandoned it.
beats.visual: B-roll: THE CANCELLATION MAZE
beats.question: What does the cancellation flow do?
beats.reveal: Page after page: confirms, reasons to stay, smaller continue buttons than abandon buttons.
beats.footage: computer screen with form, mouse clicking, website menu

beats.name: ILIAD
beats.vo: Internally, Amazon employees had a name for this sequence. Iliad.
beats.visual: Closing payoff card — ILIAD
beats.question: What did Amazon employees call it?
beats.reveal: Iliad — a name for the sequence that would not end.

beats.name: A TEN-YEAR WAR
beats.vo: They named it after Homer's epic. A poem about a war that lasted ten years. That is not an accident of translation or a coincidence of naming. Somebody inside Amazon looked at the path a customer had to walk to stop paying, and the story it reminded them of was one that famously would not end. They named it, and they kept it.
beats.visual: B-roll: A TEN-YEAR WAR
beats.text: A WAR THAT LASTED TEN YEARS
beats.question: Why the name Iliad?
beats.reveal: Somebody inside Amazon saw a path that famously would not end — and they kept it.
beats.footage: antique book pages, library stacks, epic manuscript

beats.name: SEP 25, 2025
beats.vo: On the twenty-fifth of September, 2025, in the middle of what was expected to be a month-long jury trial, Amazon settled.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — SEP 25, 2025
beats.question: How did the case end?
beats.reveal: Mid-trial, Amazon settled.
beats.footage: federal courthouse, judge's gavel, settlement document

beats.name: $2.5 BILLION
beats.vo: Two and a half billion dollars. One billion of that was a civil penalty — the largest ever imposed for violating an FTC rule. The remaining one and a half billion was earmarked for refunds to customers who'd been enrolled without meaningfully agreeing to it.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — $2.5 BILLION
beats.question: How big was the settlement?
beats.reveal: $2.5B: $1B civil penalty — largest ever for an FTC rule — $1.5B refunds.

beats.name: ADOBE SUED TOO
beats.vo: Amazon was not alone. In June 2024, the Department of Justice sued Adobe — the same Adobe — over the cancellation terms attached to its most common subscription plan. The allegation was that Adobe buried an early termination fee where customers wouldn't see it: in fine print, behind optional text boxes and links that the government said were designed to go unnoticed.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — ADOBE SUED TOO
beats.question: Was Amazon alone?
beats.reveal: June 2024: DOJ sued Adobe over a buried early-termination fee hidden in fine print.
beats.footage: contract fine print, magnifying glass, legal document

beats.name: THE FEE
beats.vo: The fee itself was fifty percent of everything remaining on the contract. So a customer who signed up for what looked like a monthly plan, and tried to leave in month four, discovered that leaving cost half of the eight months they thought they were walking away from. Adobe paid seventy-five million dollars to settle it.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — THE FEE
beats.question: What was the hidden fee?
beats.reveal: Half of the remaining contract — month four, leaving cost half of eight months. Adobe paid $75M.

beats.name: THE SAME UNDERLYING THING
beats.vo: Two of the largest companies in America, both penalised, in under two years, for the same underlying thing: making it hard to stop paying.
beats.visual: Two-sided contradiction card — THE SAME UNDERLYING THING
beats.question: What did both cases share?
beats.reveal: Two of the largest companies, penalised within two years, for making it hard to stop paying.

beats.name: SOMEBODY WROTE A RULE
beats.vo: Which raises the obvious question. If the government is winning these cases — if the penalties are this large, and the practice is this well documented — then surely somebody finally wrote a rule. Somebody did.
beats.visual: B-roll: SOMEBODY WROTE A RULE
beats.question: If the cases win, what next?
beats.reveal: The obvious question — and somebody did.
beats.footage: government document, gavel, law books

beats.name: CLICK-TO-CANCEL
beats.vo: It was called click-to-cancel. The idea was almost aggressively simple: if you can start a subscription in two clicks on a website, you must be able to end it in about two clicks on the same website. No phone call. No retention maze. No Iliad. It was not a radical rule. It was a symmetry rule. Whatever effort the company demands to begin, it can demand to end — and no more.
beats.visual: Two-sided contradiction card — CLICK-TO-CANCEL
beats.question: What did click-to-cancel demand?
beats.reveal: Symmetry: whatever effort to begin, no more to end.

beats.name: THE CHALLENGE
beats.vo: Companies fought it hard, and the trade groups behind the challenge included some of the largest advertising and industry associations in the country.
beats.visual: Chronological timeline — THE CHALLENGE
beats.question: Who opposed the rule?
beats.reveal: Companies and the largest trade associations fought it hard.

beats.name: JULY 8, 2025
beats.vo: On the eighth of July, 2025 — days before the rule was due to take effect — the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals struck it down. Entirely.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — JULY 8, 2025
beats.question: What happened days before the rule took effect?
beats.reveal: The Eighth Circuit struck it down. Entirely.
beats.footage: federal courthouse, court ruling document, gavel

beats.name: NOT ABOUT THE RULE
beats.vo: And here's the detail worth sitting with. The court did not rule that click-to-cancel was wrong. It did not find that the rule was unfair to businesses, or that consumers didn't need it, or that the FTC lacked the authority to regulate subscriptions.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — NOT ABOUT THE RULE
beats.question: Did the court reject the rule's substance?
beats.reveal: No — the FTC failed to carry out a required preliminary regulatory analysis.
beats.footage: law books, regulatory analysis, government building

beats.name: PROCEDURE
beats.vo: It struck the rule down on procedure. The FTC, the court held, had failed to carry out a preliminary regulatory analysis of the rule's costs and benefits — a step it was required to complete before finalising it. A paperwork failure. Years of rulemaking, vacated days before the deadline, because of a missing analysis.
beats.visual: Closing payoff card — PROCEDURE
beats.question: What killed the rule?
beats.reveal: A paperwork failure — years of rulemaking vacated days before the deadline.

beats.name: 2026: NO FEDERAL RULE
beats.vo: So as of right now, in 2026, there is no federal click-to-cancel rule in effect in the United States. The FTC has begun the process again — it's filed the early paperwork to write a new version — and individual states have their own laws, and enforcement actions like the Amazon and Adobe cases still happen one company at a time. But the general rule, the one that would have applied to everybody at once, does not exist.
beats.visual: Chronological timeline — 2026: NO FEDERAL RULE
beats.question: What is the status in 2026?
beats.reveal: No federal click-to-cancel rule in effect; FTC restarting; states have their own laws.

beats.name: THE FRICTION IS STILL LEGAL
beats.vo: Which means the friction is still legal. The retention screens are legal. The cancellation flow that takes six pages is legal. The plan that's easy to start on your phone and requires a phone call to end is legal.
beats.visual: Document/evidence on paper background — THE FRICTION IS STILL LEGAL
beats.question: What does no federal rule mean?
beats.reveal: Retention screens, six-page flows, phone-call cancellation — still legal.
beats.footage: phone call, customer service line, cancellation website

beats.name: NOT AN OVERSIGHT
beats.vo: Not an oversight. Not a loophole nobody noticed. A deliberate, documented, profitable design — that a court reviewed, and left in place.
beats.visual: Closing payoff card — NOT AN OVERSIGHT
beats.question: Is this an oversight?
beats.reveal: A deliberate, documented, profitable design — reviewed, and left in place.

beats.name: GO BACK TO WHERE THIS STARTED
beats.vo: Go back to where this started. Twenty point eight million members. Room for a few hundred at a time. A business that works precisely because the overwhelming majority of the people paying for it are not there.
beats.visual: B-roll: GO BACK TO WHERE THIS STARTED
beats.question: Why return to the empty gym?
beats.reveal: The business works because the people paying are not there.
beats.footage: empty gym interior, dim lighting, single treadmill

beats.name: THE LINK
beats.vo: For most of economic history, a company made money by giving you something. If it stopped delivering, you stopped paying, and that link was the entire discipline of the thing.
beats.visual: Two-sided contradiction card — THE LINK
beats.question: What kept old business honest?
beats.reveal: If it stopped delivering, you stopped paying — that link was the discipline.

beats.name: THE SEVERED LINK
beats.vo: The subscription economy severed that link. Now the payment continues on its own, and it keeps continuing until you take deliberate action to stop it — action the company has every financial reason to make slightly harder than you can be bothered with.
beats.visual: Rising line chart, paper background — THE SEVERED LINK
beats.question: What did subscriptions break?
beats.reveal: The payment continues on its own until you act — action the company makes harder than you can be bothered with.

beats.name: THE $133 GAP REFRAMED
beats.vo: That's what the hundred and thirty-three dollar gap actually is. It isn't a survey artefact, and it isn't evidence that people are bad with money. It's the measured output of a system built to convert attention into revenue, where your inattention is the raw material.
beats.visual: One number, paper background — THE $133 GAP REFRAMED
beats.question: What is the $133 gap really?
beats.reveal: The measured output of a system built to convert attention into revenue.

beats.name: THE ONLY USEFUL THING
beats.vo: So here's the only useful thing to do with any of this. Open your banking app. Search your statements for the last twelve months — not one month, twelve — and filter for anything charged in the same amount on roughly the same date. Every one of those is a decision you made once and have been renewing silently ever since.
beats.visual: B-roll: THE ONLY USEFUL THING
beats.question: What can you do with this?
beats.reveal: Search twelve months of statements for same-amount, same-date charges.
beats.footage: bank statements, phone with banking app, receipts

beats.name: KEEP WHAT YOU WANT
beats.vo: Some of them you'll want to keep. That's fine. That's a choice. Right now, for most people, it isn't. It's just the last thing they happened to agree to, still running.
beats.visual: Icon card — KEEP WHAT YOU WANT
beats.question: Do you have to cancel everything?
beats.reveal: Some you'll keep — that's fine. That's a choice.

beats.name: FINAL THESIS / HARD STOP
beats.vo: The point is that it should be a choice.
beats.visual: Closing payoff card — FINAL THESIS / HARD STOP
beats.text: THE POINT IS THAT IT SHOULD BE A CHOICE.
beats.reveal: It should be a choice — right now it's just the last thing you agreed to, still running.
